sense: at a later time, not now

terms.comment: After now, or after whatever has just been spoken of: posteā vīderō, I’ll look into it later. For “in a little while” the spoken word is mox; see in a little while.

evidence: Plaut. Epid. 656: cētera haec posterius faxō scībis, ubi erit ōtium
Cic. Att. 6.1.19: vērum haec posterius et cōram fortasse commodius
terms.comment: How a speaker puts a thing off to another time. Cicero drops a subject in his letters with sed haec posterius, but more of that later (Fam. 12.23, 15.16).

terms.gloss: later than one should, later than expected; too late
evidence: Cic. Fam. 14.10: scrīpsī ad Pompōnium sērius quam oportuit
terms.comment: The comparative of “late”, not of “after”: it measures against the right time or against someone else (sērius quam oportuit, later than I should have). It does not answer “not now, later”.

phrases.latin: abī intrō ac jubē huic aquam calefierī; cētera haec posterius faxō scībis, ubi erit ōtium
phrases.english: go in and have water heated for her; the rest I’ll tell you later, when there’s time
Not now; we’ll do it later.

sources: Lewis & Short: postea · Lewis & Short: posterus · Lewis & Short: serus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 337.
